text.p: These are the leading stories in Serbian and Montenegrin press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified them nor does it vouch for their accuracy.
-- SERBIA --
POLITIKA
- Deputy Serbian prime minister Ratko Markovic said the draft law on self-rule would more precisely define municipal and cities' authorities.

- Yugoslav ambassador to Moscow Danilo Markovic said Yugoslavia was not satisfied with the trade between the two countries which in 1996 stood at some $800 million. Yugoslavia targets $3-3.5 billion in bilateral trade by 2000.

- The federal government said it was necessary to establish and consolidate balance of public spending in the country and to intensify efforts for the country's return to international financial and trade organisations and institutions.
- Montenegrin power company Elektroprivreda Crne Gore offers concessions for four hydro-electric power stations to foreign investors.
- Serbian government has prepared a programme for economic and financial consolidation of construction firms to contribute to their development and help them adjust to market conditions.
- Experts of the Institute for Foreign Trade warn drastic decline of imports could cause fall in production and slower exports.
- Yugoslav government gets home page on Internet.
NASA BORBA
- Zoran Djindjic, the Democratic party leader said the break-up of Serbia's opposition coalition Zajedno would not be a tragedy.
- Stevan Djordjevic, leader of Serbia's health workers' trade union said strike would continue until all demands were met. No positive development in talks with the government.
- Serbia's state administration, judiciary and social organisation workers' trade union issue warning on low wages.
- Yugoslav secretary for information Goran Matic said the draft of the new information law expected by the end of summer, announced forming of federal state television.
- Milan Mandic, president of the Australian-Serbian chamber said delays of privatisation slows down foreign investment.
- Australian fast-food chain in Yugoslavia soon.

- Some 80 percent of foreign currency depositors are over 75 years old and the question is if they would live to be paid out their savings in 13 years as proposed by the draft of the law on old foreig currency savings.
- Yugoslavia, Japan upgrade their relations to ambassadorial level.
-- MONTENEGRO --
POBJEDA
- Montenegrin parliament passed a law on security council, a security service watchdog body, despite opposition claims that the law is non-constitutional.
- The U.S. Ministry of Finance released five Montenegrin vessels which were blocked under sanctions regime in U.S. ports of New York, Baltimore and New Orleans.
- As of June 1 train passenger service between Podgorica and Niksic will be abolished. Bad state of railways will cause at least 20 minutes delays on Bar-Belgrade train.
- The conflict in the People's Party was organised by Belgrade, said party deputy chairman Predrag Drecun. -- Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 222 4254
